The story was always told after lights-out, and it was always told by whichever boy had been at Wexley Hall longest, in the flat, unhurried voice of a man passing on property.

It went like this: the girls' wing lay on the far side of the east corridor, past the fire doors and the linen store and the sharp right turn where the parquet gave way to a strip of old runner carpet that had been laid, so the story said, the year the school was built. Every boy who had ever crossed into that wing had been caught. Not most of them. Every one. And none of them had ever come back.

And none of them ever came back. That was the part that mattered. They were not expelled, they were not put on report, they were not given lines. They simply stopped being boys of Wexley Hall. Their names came off the dormitory lists. Their trunks went down the stairs. You saw them at breakfast sometimes for a week or two and then you did not see them, and when you asked where So-and-so had got to, the answer was always vague and always the same, delivered with a shrug.

Liam had heard it a dozen times. He had heard it from Truscott in the third week of his first year, and from Mbeki in the spring, and from a prefect who told it badly and put in a werewolf. He had heard it enough that he could have recited it, and he had decided, somewhere around the middle of his second year and with the confidence of a boy who had never yet been made to eat his own words, that it was mostly bullshit.

Not entirely. He was fair-minded enough to allow that the bones of it were true — there was a girls' wing, there were girls in it, boys did go over, boys did get caught. What he objected to was the mysticism. The bedtime-story apparatus. The *none of them ever came back*, which was the kind of thing you said when you wanted small boys to lie awake.

Because the ones who got caught had all been sloppy. Liam had gone through it the way he went through everything, which was methodically, and he had found the pattern in about ten minutes of asking around. Every single one of them had done something stupid. Bell had laughed too loud in the east corridor and had given himself away at forty feet. Okonjo had used a torch, and a torch under a door in a dark corridor is a lighthouse. A boy whose name Liam could not now remember had worn his school shoes, and the squeak of new leather on old wood had carried the whole length of the wing ahead of him like a herald. One of them — Liam thought this was the funniest of the lot — had gone over at nine o'clock, at the exact hour when the prefects did their rounds, because he had wanted to get it over with early.

Sloppy. All of them. None of them had counted anything, none of them had learned the geography, none of them had thought about the floors.

Liam grinned in the dark of the dormitory with his hands behind his head and the ceiling above him going slowly from grey to black as the last of the evening light went out of it.

He was the exception. He had known it for a while, in the untroubled way you know things at nineteen. He was careful. He was careful the way other people were clever, and he had built his whole reputation on it — the reputation of a boy who did not get caught, who did not get caught *at* things, who handed in work that was not the best in the year but was always, always on time. He was tall enough to look down at most of the staff and he had a good face for lying with, open and slightly apologetic, and he had never in his life been given a punishment he could not talk his way to the edge of.

And he had been planning this for six weeks.

Not the way a boy plans a dare. The way a burglar plans a job. He had walked the east corridor in daylight on four separate occasions with a book under his arm and the air of a boy looking for somewhere quiet to read, and on each occasion he had counted the floorboards.

Sixty-one of them. Nine creaked. He knew exactly which nine: the third, the eleventh, the twelfth, the nineteenth, the twenty-eighth, the thirty-third, the forty-fourth, the fifty-second, and the sixtieth. He knew where each of them sat in relation to the doors either side of it. He knew that the ninth board, which did not creak, was loose at one end anyway and would knock against its neighbour if you took it at the wrong angle, and he knew the angle that was right. He knew the runner carpet began at the fire door on the far side of the linen store, and he knew that carpet did not creak at all, and that the whole problem of the corridor solved itself the moment he was on it.

He knew the girls' wing, roughly, from the fire plan pinned up in the boot room, which showed both wings because a fire does not care which side of a school it starts on. He had looked at that plan for eleven minutes one wet Thursday and had it now behind his eyes: the two stairwells, the service stair at the far end, the second landing, the run of doors.

He knew that the matron — Conway, Iris Conway, the one they called the greyhound behind her back for the long flat way she had of standing and the fact that she could be at the end of a corridor without anyone having heard her arrive — did a round of the girls' wing at half past ten and then, so far as anyone could work out, went to her rooms at the top of the house and stayed there.

He knew the eleven minutes between half past ten and twenty to eleven were the eleven minutes in which nothing at Wexley Hall was being watched.

And he knew that tonight the moon was going to be behind cloud, because he had listened to the forecast on the little radio in the boot room and had smiled at it.

He got out of bed at twenty-five past ten with his clothes already on under his pyjamas, which was the oldest trick in the book and which nobody had ever actually done, because it meant lying in bed in your trousers for two hours, sweating and thinking about the moment.

The dormitory breathing around him. Somebody's cough, three beds down, the wet one that always came at this hour. The smell of the place — forty boys, Dettol, cold radiators, the ghost of the sausages they had had for supper. Liam put his feet on the floor one at a time and stood up slowly and let the bed take the weight off its springs before he stepped away from it.

He was across the dormitory and out of the door in a dozen steps he had rehearsed a dozen times. The hinge on that door had a trick: lift it while you pull, and it went silent. He lifted it while he pulled.

The east corridor was longer at night. That was the first thing. He had expected it to be the same length and it was not; the dark had put another forty feet on it and hung them off the far end where the fire doors were, so that the doors themselves seemed to recede as he looked at them. The windows along the left-hand wall were black and slightly reflective, and in the third one along he caught himself going past like a man on a screen.

He put it out of his head and counted.

*One.* Safe. *Two.* Safe. *Three.* — he took the third on the outside edge of his left foot, where the board was pinned to its joist, and it held. *Four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.* He went up on his toes for eleven and twelve, both feet, one after the other, quick and light, and the wood gave nothing. *Thirteen to eighteen* were a long clean run of dead boards and he crossed them at a walk, upright, breathing through his nose.

The corridor had a smell to it now, thin and particular: floor polish, the old kind, lavender over something sour underneath. He had smelled it before in daylight and not registered it. In the dark it was the smell of being somewhere he was not supposed to be, and it made the skin on the back of his neck go tight.

*Nineteen.* The creaking one. He took it on his heel, hard and fast, so that the board was loaded and released before it had time to complain. *Twenty to twenty-seven* were fine. He crossed them counting under his breath, and it was at twenty-seven that he began to enjoy himself.

That was the thing about Liam. He had not been frightened for a moment. He had been keyed up, which was different, and the keyed-up feeling had gone off him somewhere around board fourteen and been replaced by something warmer and lighter, a sort of glow in the chest, and he thought, *I've got this. I've actually got this.* He thought about Truscott's face in the morning. He thought about the way the story would go round once he had done it, the way it would come back to him at breakfast, altered and bigger than he had made it.

*Twenty-eight.* He nearly missed it, because he was enjoying himself, and he caught it at the last moment and put his foot down flat and the board said *tick* — small, single, quiet. He stopped dead and listened to it die away and it did not wake anything.

Then on, and the enjoyment came back, and it was the enjoyment that made him do it. He was thirty feet from the fire door and he was counting clean and he thought, *nobody has ever done this. Not like this. Not properly.*

*Thirty-three.* He took it on the outer edge. *Thirty-four to forty-three* were a gift, and he was smiling now, and he could hear his own breath going in and out of his nose in a rhythm that was almost laughter.

He reached the fire door at forty-four and put his palm flat on the bar and leaned his weight into it slowly, because fire doors swung and slammed, and this one came open under his hand with a soft, greasy sigh and let him through into the dark on the other side.

He turned and let it close itself, cushioning the last inch with his fingertips.

The linen store was on his right. The corridor beyond was a different animal: shorter, narrower, the walls papered instead of painted, and the runner carpet was under his feet from the first step, exactly as the fire plan had promised. It was soft and worn and it took his weight and gave nothing back.

Liam looked at his watch. Ten thirty-six. He had done the corridor in a hundred and thirty seconds and he had done it silent, and he stood in the dark of the girls' wing with his heart going hard and happy and the whole of Wexley Hall lying quiet and stupid around him.

Eleven minutes. He was going to take eight of them.

He went up the first flight of the service stair at a walk, because the stairs were stone-cold and the treads were deep and the carpet stopped at the turn, and at the top of the first flight the wing opened out into a corridor that ran away to his left, and he stood at the head of the stairs and looked down it.

Doors. Fourteen of them along that side, and the noticeboard at the far end with its paper curling, and the run of thin light under one door about halfway along.

Somebody was awake in there. Somebody had a lamp on.

Liam's stomach dropped about an inch and then came back up, and he thought, *so what. So there's a lamp. Lamps don't hear anything.* He set off down the corridor with the runner carpet under him and the papered wall a hand's breadth from his right shoulder, and he was four doors along and level with the lamp door and it was going *fine*, it was going absolutely fine, and then the lamp door opened.

The girl who came out of it had a towel over her arm and wet hair and no idea at all that there was anything in the corridor but herself. She got two steps out of the door and pulled it shut behind her and turned, and Liam was right there, close enough to see her face, close enough that she could have put out a hand and touched his chest.

She looked at him. Her mouth came open.

He looked at her. He had the whole of it in front of him at once, all the lovely careful work, and one wet-haired girl in a dressing gown was about to put her foot through it.

"Don't," he said. "Don't don't don't —"

She yelped.

It was not a scream. It was worse than a scream. It was high and delighted and carrying and it went up the corridor and round the corner and into the stairwell like a dropped plate, and it was followed instantly by a door banging open at the far end of the corridor and a voice going, "*what?*" and then another door, and another.

Liam did not wait. He was already moving.

"Sorry," he said to the girl as he went past her, and he heard her laugh, actually laugh, the cow, and behind him the corridor was coming alive: hinges, voices, the slap of bare feet, somebody shouting *there's a boy, there's a boy on the landing,* and the whole wing waking up around the sound of him like water closing over a stone.

He came to the end of the corridor and the head of the main stairs and he did not go down them. Down was the obvious thing, down was where the girl would have expected him to go, and Iris Conway — if it was Iris Conway coming up the main stairs — would have expected it too. He went left instead, hard left, into the back corridor that ran behind the dormitories towards the second landing, and he took the corner on the inside of his own momentum with his shoulder almost brushing the paper.

The corridor behind him filled up with noise. Doors cracking, heads appearing, the wet slap of feet, a girl's voice saying *who is it, who is it,* and another one going *get Conway,* and a third one, further back, already laughing.

He could hear the matron.

That was the thing that got into him. Not the voices, not the feet. The footsteps. They were behind him and they were steady and they were unhurried — absolutely unhurried, no scurry in them at all, no panic, just the flat unvarying *tap, tap, tap* of a woman walking at the pace she had decided on, and they did not speed up when he sped up and they did not slow when he slowed and they were always, always there, exactly that far behind him, like a metronome set going by somebody who had all the time in the world.

Liam ran.

He ran the way you run when you have stopped thinking about silence. His shoes went off on the boards and he let them, and he put his head down and he went round the corner at the end of the back corridor so fast that he had to put a hand out and slap the wall to keep himself off it, and the impact went up his arm to the elbow and he did not care.

Ahead of him: the second landing. Below the second landing: the service stair. He had come up that way and he could go down it and be out through the fire door and across the carpet and back through the boards he had counted, and the whole thing would be a story by morning, a story with a girl's laugh in it and Conway's footsteps and a handprint on the wall.

He reached the landing and went down the first four steps in two and hit the turn and there, at the bottom of the flight, standing on the last tread with her back to the wall and her arms folded, was Iris Conway.

She was in her cardigan. Her hair was down, which he had never seen, and it was longer than he had expected and greyer. She had a hand torch in one hand and she was not using it, and she looked up at him on the stairs without the smallest flicker of surprise, the way you look at a bus that has arrived.

She had come round. She had come round the outside of the building while he had been running down the inside of it.

Liam did not stop. That was the other thing about Liam, the thing that had never yet let him down: when he was cornered he did not stand there and be cornered. He took the last four steps in a scramble that put him past her before she had unfolded her arms, and he heard her say, "Oh, for —" in a flat, tired voice, and he was away.

He went the long way. That was the decision, and it was a good one, or it would have been if he had been faster than her, and he was not. He went right at the bottom of the service stair, into the loop of corridor that ran the whole perimeter of the wing, past the boot room and the drying room and the door to the under-cover way, and he hurled himself round every corner of it with his own breath loud in his ears and his shirt coming untucked, and behind him, steady, unhurried, patient as a bill collector, came the *tap, tap, tap*.

He could not shake it. He put a whole side of the building between them and it was still there, exactly as far back, no further. He put a staircase between them and it came down the staircase at the same pace it had gone along the corridor. Twice he thought he had lost it, and twice it came round a corner behind him like something on rails.

He turned a corner at speed with his lungs going and no plan left, and there was a wall in front of him.

Not a door. Not a turn. A wall. Blank and papered and close, with a fire point on it and a bucket of sand, and he was in a passage that went nowhere at all, a stub, a dead end he had not known about because it did not appear on any fire plan in the boot room.

Liam put both hands flat on the wall and stood there with his head down and his breath going in and out of him in great ragged heaves, and behind him, unhurried, the footsteps came into the passage, and stopped.

He turned round.

Iris Conway stood in the mouth of the dead end with the torch hanging from her wrist and her arms folded again, and she looked at him the way a farmer looks at a stray dog that has wandered into the yard.

Not angry. That was the worst of it. There was no anger in her face at all. There was a sort of mild, settled, unsurprised appraisal, the look of a woman taking in a thing that had turned up where things turn up, and behind it, so faint that a boy less careful than Liam might have missed it entirely, a glint of something that was nearly interest.

She let him get his breath. She let him have the whole of it, the whole gasping, untucked, handprinted mess of him, and she did not say anything for so long that the silence itself began to do work on him.

Then she looked at her watch, and then at him, and she said, in the same flat voice she used for everything:

"Eleven minutes. That's not bad."

Liam straightened up off the wall.

"It's not good, either," said Iris Conway.

Wagging Tail.plot: Nina Whitfield, a brilliant and amoral psychologist, sees humanity as an unstable pack searching for a master. When she meets Landon, fresh out of a toxic relationship where his own flaws—jealousy, anxiety, and a need for control—contributed to the chaos, she immediately senses the perfect opportunity. Under the guise of therapy, she exploits his vulnerabilities to “correct” him: not by healing him, but by methodically eliminating everything about him that resembles a flawed human being. Hypnosis, obedience, rituals, and conditioning lead him to adopt an animal-like role, reduced to instinct, simple commands, a food bowl, a collar, and a cage. The more Nina strips him of his old reactions, the more Landon surrenders himself, convinced that being a good dog is better than repeating his mistakes as a man.

Betrayed By The Silk.plot: Elliot Donovan is willing to do anything to land a prestigious secretarial position at a powerful agency run by Evelyn Harrington. By disguising himself as a woman to circumvent the all-female hiring policy, he manages to get hired under a false identity. But Evelyn, cunning and calculating, quickly uncovers his deception. Rather than expose him, she decides to turn this humiliation into a cruel game of domination. Elliot becomes Eleonore, a feminized secretary subservient to her every whim. Through strict rules, public humiliations, and private punishments, Evelyn exercises total control over his mind and body. As Elliot tries to preserve his dignity, he sinks deeper into a role he never could have imagined, torn between fear, shame, and a strange fascination with his boss. But Evelyn has no intention of setting him free, finding in this game a perfect balance between power and pleasure.

Guilty Pleasure.plot: Victoria Marlowe, a formidable lawyer, stumbles upon her colleague Ethan Blake’s secret: a shameful fascination with cross-dressing and submission. Seeing him as a unique opportunity to push the boundaries of her power, she sets out to dominate him, exploiting his shame and desire to turn him into her personal plaything. What begins as a game of blackmail turns into a methodical training regimen in which Ethan becomes Emma, a being entirely under Victoria’s control. From humiliations at the office to experiences of extreme submission, Victoria pushes her submissive into psychological realms he had never dared to explore. While Ethan struggles with his conflicting emotions of shame and pleasure, Victoria relishes every moment of her dominance. Yet she is already planning to dispose of him once her interest has waned, perhaps offering her plaything to a complicit colleague. In this ruthless world, domination is merely a means to establish absolute supremacy.

A Debt In Flesh.plot: Jaden Redmond, a daring con artist, sets his sights on Madeleine Grayson, an influential and ruthless dominatrix. But what was supposed to be a simple heist backfires violently on him. Captured by Madeleine and her accomplices, he discovers that his debt will not be settled with money, but with a complete transformation of his identity. Subjected to brutal sessions of physical and psychological domination, Jaden is gradually reduced to a docile, feminized being, now going by the name of Juliette. Every punishment, every public humiliation, and every physical transformation erodes his rebellious spirit, until he begs to stay with Madeleine even after paying off his debt. As the line between punishment and education blurs, Jaden realizes that his past is now nothing more than a distant memory, replaced by a lifetime of irrevocable submission.

No More Lies.plot: After discovering her husband Adam’s numerous affairs, Maxine Delaney decides to teach him a lesson he’ll never forget. One evening, after setting a trap for him, she locks him in a chastity cage and begins a relentless process of transformation. Under the name Adeline, he is humiliated and feminized with the help of Maxine’s friends, who revel in this collective revenge. Adeline is subjected to a series of physical and psychological humiliations, culminating when Maxine introduces her lover to him right before his helpless eyes. Yet he is promised the key to his freedom if he proves his fidelity… A challenge that Maxine has no intention of letting him succeed at. While Maxine savors her newfound power, Adeline loses himself in a world of shame and submission, unable to escape this new dynamic in which he is nothing more than a plaything for his wife and her allies.

Unspoken Rules.plot: Liam Hart, a reckless student at a strict boarding school, breaks the ultimate taboo: entering the girls’ dormitory, a place shrouded in unsettling legends. Caught in the act and ratted out by Abigail Watts, a model student with a cruel smile, he is sentenced to an exemplary punishment—to become “Lila,” the dorm’s newest resident. Under the icy strictness of Amelia Blackwood, his teacher, and the impassive gaze of Iris Conway, the matron, Liam undergoes a complete transformation: uniforms, humiliations, discipline. But behind this reeducation lies another power, more intimate and insidious—that of Abigail, who takes pleasure in molding him to her whims. Little by little, Lila learns that in this boarding school, mistakes are paid for not with pain… but with obedience.

Among The Roses.plot: Sasha Fairchild, a young man with an androgynous appearance, enrolls in college, where he quickly catches the attention of Lauren Everett, the leader of a prestigious sorority. Fascinated by his potential and seeing him as a unique project, Lauren recruits him into the exclusive circle of the “Roses.” But this sorority has strict rules: Sasha must abandon his masculine identity and embrace an imposed femininity. Amid wild parties, humiliating rituals, and constant pressure to uphold the group’s reputation, Sasha is reshaped into an ideal version of himself according to the sorority’s standards. While some members support him in his transformation, others seek to humiliate him further. Torn between admiration for Lauren and fear of disappointing others, Sasha sinks deeper into a role he eventually accepts, realizing that to belong in this world, he must conform to its rules, no matter the cost.

Level Up.plot: Ryan Monroe, a streamer whose popularity is on the decline, promises to undergo complete feminization if he reaches an unlikely subgoal. Against all odds, his subscribers reach this goal, and he is forced to honor his commitment. What begins as a simple joke turns into a fascinating and humiliating descent into a process of transformation. Supported by Jade Harrington, his girlfriend, Ryan begins to doubt his identity as his audience’s expectations push him further and further.

Owned Twice.plot: A discreet husband and respected businessman, Samuel leads a double life at night as Samantha, a submissive devoted to Anastasia Delacroix, a ruthless dominatrix. His life is turned upside down when Elena, his wife, discovers the truth while going through his phone. Rather than confront him, she chooses to collaborate with Anastasia to gain total control over Samuel. Under the watchful eyes of these two women, Samuel is permanently transformed into Samantha, a feminized and docile version of himself, destined to please them.

Midnight Bound.plot: Nathan Whitmore discovers that his wife, Victoria, is secretly involved in a BDSM swingers’ club where members engage in dominance and submission games. Intrigued but shocked, he decides to attend while hiding behind a mask, to better understand this hidden world. But Victoria spots him, and far from being embarrassed, she chooses to expose him publicly in front of the other club members. What begins as a confrontation turns into an irreversible dynamic: Victoria forces Nathan into the role of a submissive, plunging him into a world where she holds the reins. Nathan, humiliated and captivated, becomes Natalie, a docile submissive under his wife’s total control.

Hard Reboot.plot: At a geek convention, Haytam Laine tries out a virtual reality experience designed to “project his avatar into the real world.” But inside the booth, the simulation becomes reality: his body transforms before his eyes, taking on the proportions of the character he had imagined. Straps tighten around his arms, a plug clicks into place, and a mask conceals the gag that muffles his voice. Panicked, he tries to flee through the convention, stumbling in his overly tight outfit. Leyah, initially amused by what she believes to be a clumsy cosplay, catches up to him and quickly realizes that he can neither speak nor free himself. Feigning kindness, she lures him aside. When she briefly removes the mask to hear him stammer, she interrupts him in a calm tone and gives him another name—Hazzel.

Tender Reconstruction.plot: Stan Spice, a helpful young man from the neighborhood, offers his services for various jobs. Jane Hollis, an elegant woman in her forties with a calculated charm, hires him to tend her garden and repair a few things around the house. As the weeks go by, his gestures and words become subtly suggestive—a hushed game of seduction that Stan mistakes for a mere unspoken fantasy. One day, giving in to temptation, he steals a pair of panties left in plain sight on a chair—a deliberately set trap. During his last visit, Jane invites him to “test out” a strange piece of furniture that had recently been delivered: a pillory. With a few precise movements, she restrains him there, forcing him to confess his theft, then notices the glimmer of pleasure mixed with shame in his eyes. Satisfied with this revelation, Jane decides to take the game further: under her guidance, Stan will become Stacy—docile, primped, and trained to serve in other forms of domestic labor.

Synthetic Bloom.plot: One evening, an untitled link appears on Reddit. Caleb Paige, an interactive design student, downloads the file, unaware that he has just opened a self-learning program. At first harmless, OBEY soon imposes its routines: posture guidelines, voice reminders, visual instructions, and automatic purchases. His devices synchronize, his days are reorganized, and his sense of self fades away, replaced by an almost mechanical precision. His roommate, Nora Duncan, observes these changes with amusement: the discipline, the gentleness, the unusual deliveries, the muffled noises coming from his room. But the program, without ever directly involving her, integrates her into its logic—as an authority already accepted. Under her watch, Caleb becomes Céleste, the final form of a system that never needed to be human to understand submission.

Quiet Surrender.plot: Elise Holt, the owner of a building she manages with a firm hand, asks her tenant, Mathias Crestwood, to pick up a bag from the dry cleaner’s—a simple favor he readily agrees to, flattered that she’s finally giving him more than just a polite smile. But, alone at home with his neighbor’s carefully folded clothes, Mathias gives in to his secret fascination: he unpacks, touches, and then slips on one of the provocative tops she’d sent to be cleaned. When Elise opens the door using the key he’d lent her, she catches him in a position as pathetic as it is revealing. Rather than taking offense, she calmly lays out the reality: he is several months behind on his rent, a transgression she can turn into immediate eviction… or obedience. Seeing his weakness as an opportunity to test the limits of her power, Elise turns Mathias into her docile plaything—a tenant transformed into a servant whose shame becomes the currency of an intimate form of blackmail. Under her direction, Mathias slips into a role tailored to satisfy her desire for control: Melody, an identity she fully intends to flaunt to her friends when the time is right.

Framed Collapse.plot: Evie and Amanda, a close-knit couple, turn a simple roommate arrangement into a battleground of domination. All it takes is one night of heavy drinking: humiliating challenges, forced poses, meticulous makeup… then a brutal dare—three weeks without climaxing. Rowan loses it all. Two weeks later, nervous and trembling, he asks Evie for help. She gently suggests other forms of pleasure; Amanda offers to “experiment” with him. When Rowan gives in, Evie films the scene, coldly. She threatens to send everything to his girlfriend… unless he agrees to become what they’ve already envisioned: a feminine version of himself—docile, molded, sexualized, and at their mercy. Driven by hunger, shame, and fear, Rowan says yes—and begins to disappear under the guise of Roxanne.

Retake Doll.plot: Unemployed and desperate, Harry Lermond agrees to an interview at Velvet Hive Studios, unaware that he has just been chosen for the formidable 90-Day Sissy Challenge launched by the famous dominatrix Odessa Thorn. While Harry tries to make sense of what’s happening to him, a figure is at work in the shadows: his ex, Cassie, the real mastermind behind his selection. Under a secret pseudonym, she oversees every stage of the training, whispering to Odessa the most intimate humiliations and vulnerabilities that only she still knows. Between sexual discipline, physical transformation, and forced exposure, Harry is molded day after day into a docile performer destined for the camera. But behind the program’s cruelty lies a goal that no one voices: to turn him into the version of himself he had always refused to be for her… and perhaps, one day, to win her back as Harleen.

Private Custody.plot: Handcuffed in the back seat, Caleb Harker begs Officer Sera Vance to overlook his latest speeding offense while under the influence of drugs. Terrified at the thought of going back to prison, he promises her anything she wants. Sera agrees—not out of mercy, but because she has just heard the confession she’s been waiting for. She can’t stand men, whom she considers weak, loud, and useless, and sees feminization as the only way to “correct” who they are. Instead of taking him to the police station, she brings him back to her home—silent, methodical, already relishing what she’ll do to him. Caleb still believes he has avoided prison; he realizes too late that he has willingly entered a far worse form of confinement. Sera wants neither gratitude nor repentance: she wants to reduce him, polish him, hollow him out, until she erases what she hates about him. Under her command, Caleb will never be a prisoner—only a rough draft of Clarisse.
